Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.

Editor’s note (November 17, 2026): This post has been updated with additional CVE information and updated guidance for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Please see the release information below for the versions that include the fixes.

Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.An attacker-controlled Git server can exploit this discrepancy to replace a clone’s .git file or directory, redirecting Git to attacker-controlled configuration or hooks.For recursive clones, this can execute attacker-controlled code during the clone. For non-recursive clones, an attacker can replace the top-level .git directory with a file pointing to attacker-controlled repository metadata. The clone can then report an error and recommend running git status in the resulting directory; following that advice can execute attacker-controlled code.The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Robert Chen reported CVE-2026-111760, which was fixed by Elijah Newren and Toon Claes, with help from Johannes Schindelin and Jeff King. Luke Martin reported CVE-2026-113408, which was fixed by Toon Claes.

pwn2addr reported CVE-2026-114466, CVE-2026-114467, and CVE-2026-114469, which were fixed by Karthik Nayak. Kaartic Sivaraam implemented the fix for CVE-2026-105437 based on a patch by Jeff King, with help from Toon Claes and Christian Couder.

Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.

#9809. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

That is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each new task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

#9808. Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad

President threatens 'tremendous tax' on overseas builds, but analysts question how restrictions would work

US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China.

Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose.

Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country."

The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said.

The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X.

We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer.

Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here."

The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week.

"We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added.

Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it.

Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January.

Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses.

Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat.

"There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register.

"So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences."

Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the cloud giants operate datacenters outside the US, such as latency and regulatory compliance.

"A buyer in Frankfurt won't wait for a page to load from Virginia. Some countries require certain data to stay inside their borders, and big European clients write it into contracts anyway," he stated.

Trump claimed that communities in America that host datacenters are "making so much money that they don't know what to do with it."

Those claimed benefits come alongside substantial public subsidies. Nonprofit organization Good Jobs First reported earlier this year that some states are losing billions in revenue because of the tax abatement schemes offered to companies to entice them to set up shop there. ®

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”.

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?

The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.

The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.

The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.

The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.

Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files: .claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and .github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:

Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.

Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.

#9805. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#9804. Everything going down at once wasn't evidence of a conspiracy – but the truth may be scarier

Rogue AI or nation-state hackers would be preferable to the amount of technical debt the past week of wobbling services laid bare

Have you or someone you love been affected by a tech outage this week? Yeah, us too.

In a week of big stories the biggest one seems to be the fact that everyone from Microsoft to the NSA was dealing with outages, and here's what might be the worst part: It doesn't seem to be AI, nor hostile countries intent on destroying our infrastructure.

Unfortunately for all of us, what the past week of outages reveal is that – as we discussed on The Kettle less than a month ago – all of our essential tech infrastructure is basically held together with duct tape and twine.Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons, and open source reporter Liam Proven to discuss what comes next, and whether we can fix any of this without tearing all of it out and starting from scratch.

A lightly edited transcript is included below:

Hi everyone and welcome to the latest episode of the Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and if you're hearing this, then that means there isn't an outage right now, which seems like that might be a lot to ask of our technology in the past week. It's been a busy week. We had Anthropic's IPO, Nvidia drama continuing, and other stuff going on. But the one thing that everyone seems to be talking about is what's become known in the zeitgeist as Outagepalooza, as it seems like everything was offline at some point in the past few days. With me to discuss the chaos and the conspiracy theories they're giving rise to is Reg cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons and our open source reporter Liam Proven. Guys, what's happening?

I've got my tinfoil hat on right now, so I'm ready.

Yes, I've had family calling me being like, my god, what's happening? Who's ending the world right now? Is it AI?

Wonderful. My mum's wardrobe door stuck this week and we found a company on the little rock in the middle of the Irish Sea that fixes sliding doors and he didn't get my emails because he's one hundred percent Microsoft and he uses Hotmail and it's Hotmail.

And when I got it through, you'd be amazed at the ramifications. I SMS'd him in the end and he got that and then was really angry because I said, "Dude, I've been trying to get you for three days. Can you at least reply and say Friday?" And he's like, "No, I've got no email, I've got no internet, I've got nothing."

My god. Yes, it's been an interesting week. So Jess, catch us up on everything that's fallen apart in the past few days. We've got quite a list growing here.

Yes. Well, we'll start with Outlook. I'm sorry, Microsoft. It was larger than just Outlook, but similar to Liam, I got this message from my dad. We were at dinner with some friends and he said, "What is going on? I haven't been able to access Outlook all day. What is happening?" So this happened last week and there was this massive Microsoft outage and ultimately, people assumed it was maybe a cyber attack. Is somebody DDoSing Microsoft? What's going on? And then a few days later, Microsoft said, "No, this was a faulty software update that we pushed back in July, and it's affecting all of our 365 services now." So that was last Thursday. Then a day later, the FAA grounded all planes.

And again, in light of Microsoft, people were still having problems with Microsoft. All the planes are grounded. At the time, we just knew it was some type of communication error. And that sounds like something that a lot of nation states would really like to hit and attack. And this one, we ultimately learned that it was due to a network upgrade. Their provider, L3Harris, was switching out the copper wiring with fiber. And this has been an ongoing project. Also, kind of seems like maybe Friday the 13th isn't the best day to undertake this.

I hadn't even thought about the fact that it was Friday the 13th that all that happened.

So we see that right after Microsoft. And there was kind of a lull over the weekend, which was nice. But then Monday first thing, customers at Chase and US Bank and other major American banks couldn't withdraw any money from their accounts. And this we find out is also due to a massive outage. Chase later said it was a software bug in an on-premises hardware system, and they said it wasn't a cyber attack. Then the next day, the classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for their internal communications went offline. This is really classified stuff that they are communicating about internally. This went offline and when something at a secretive government agency like the NSA goes offline, immediately the first thought is, "Who's attacking us?" The agency later said this was due to scheduled routine maintenance. And actually I almost forgot: Tuesday, Apple had a bunch of issues. It was affecting different services like Apple Support, iCloud, Apple Pay, and their retail stores. There were people waiting in lines because they had some tech issue that they wanted to get help with, and they're not able to get any help because Apple's offline as well. So we have all these outages at these major agencies and companies over the last week. So everybody automatically goes to, "Who's attacking us? Who is responsible for this?" What people assume to be a massive coordinated cyber attack And that wasn't the case.

Right. In pretty much every instance. Liam, Canonical was having an outage too, right?

Yes. I was going to say, we didn't notice the FAA very much in Europe, but Canonical got hit by a distributed denial of service attack. I probably don't need to spell that out. At the end of last week, just before their now semi-annual Ubuntu Summit, which is when they have a bunch of talks about what's coming up and what's new. They've been hit by a number of attacks before. It was very bad timing. Some of their services stayed up.

So this was actually attributable to an attack though.

I believe in this case it looks like it was another DDoS, but it's not the first time. It's not obvious in the open source world that sometimes big, very visible projects are actually from tiny companies. And sometimes things that don't look so important actually have huge companies behind them. But Canonical is not a very big company. And they're a hundred percent remote company. They don't really have headquarters. There's this lovely office which is part of a floor of one building in London, but not that many people work there. It's all hot desks.

It's relatively easy to take such a distributed company offline. And so it's becoming hard to say whether some of these things really are due to attacks or due to general vulnerabilities that are being maybe not even exploited, just massive scale attempts to exploit them. And it's not sometimes targeting anybody in particular. There's just a million bots trying to take down PHP and loads of things run on PHP. So you've got PHP in your infrastructure and that means you're not taken down, but your servers are struggling under the load. The number of bots that are trying to crawl all kinds of websites and things constitutes effectively a DDoS at the moment, although it's not really a true DDoS.

Right. It's not intentional. It just becomes one by volume.

So it's actually becoming a little bit moot what exactly constitutes a denial of service attack versus merely being under extremely heavy load. I'm sure that the jokes are international about phoning your bank or some other institution and getting a recorded message saying, "We're sorry, we're experiencing an unusual volume of calls at the moment. You are number forty-two in the queue." You've always got that volume of calls. It's not unusual. That's your normal volume of calls. Hire more people. That's web service now, isn't it?

Yes, gosh. But there's that. Aside from maybe the Canonical thing being a bit of an outlier in this broader discussion, it seems like there's not necessarily a single thing to blame here, right? It's very easy to immediately jump to the conclusion that this is AI. Right? They're lying to us.

Well, I think we can establish the cause under the larger umbrella of deferred maintenance because we have this aging, underfunded infrastructure. That was the case with the FAA outage, and we have all of these really old bugs in software that are just now coming to light because AI has gotten so good at finding them in a lot of either commercial projects or open source code that wasn't really built with security top of mind. And so all of these things are now happening right at once. There's this massive need to upgrade infrastructure. There's this need to patch all of these vulnerabilities really quickly before attackers reverse engineer them with AI and then exploit them. And it's creating this perfect storm that looks like it could be an attack, but it's software vulnerabilities, it's deferred maintenance, and that's at least the primary cause of all the outages.

Yes.You don't think... I mean, I'm just going to put my tinfoil hat on and say, "Well, are these people lying to us?" Are they trying to cover up another big wave of OpenAI agents crashing networks due to stupidly miscoded exercises that are escaping sandboxes?

Can I propose a rephrasing of the question?

Yes, they're lying to us, but are they lying about this?

Yes, right. And and that's the thing. I mean, it's always the that's that's always a question at the back of everybody's minds. Like over the weekend I had someone who a friend of mine, she's not involved in cybersecurity, she's not involved in government, and trying to convince me that no, this this was all part of a coordinated cyber attack. And very convinced. Um some people, there's there's a few people in the security industry who are saying, "Well, it seems that they were really quick to rush and say, 'no this was just scheduled downtime or an upgrade that we had planned.'" But the consensus from all of the security folks who are a lot smarter than I am is that no, this doesn't appear to be a coordinated cyber attack. This really does look like it has to do with a bunch of bugs being discovered in all of our interconnected systems.And this has a cascading effect across so many critical systems and services that we all use.

Right. I know you covered this in the story you wrote about the greater impact of all this. Can we expect more of this going forward? I think we probably all know the answer to that.

That raises the big question of this. I've been telling my family and my friends all along that there's not an indication that this is connected. But it was less than a month ago that the three of us were on here talking about PHP2Shell and how that basically opened the box to us realizing the entire digital sphere that we exist in is held together with duct tape and twine. Yes.

Right. And we see some real attacks too, with the refrigeration attacks and the water system attacks in America over the summer. So there are real attacks that are happening and affecting critical systems too. So it's not like these outages are occurring in a vacuum with nothing being  perpetrated by criminals, or spies, or nation-state attackers.

Yes. You think about it like the modern internet that we have... Liam, you lived on the continent for a while. So, in history, Europe was a whole bunch of very small, very isolated communities. They developed their own languages, their own culture, everything. And then they grew and they became one connected mass. But in some ways they still can't talk to each other. And I feel like that's the kind of technology that we have now. We have all these disparate systems that existed as separate entities. The FAA's 50-year-old systems didn't need to be connected to the internet and talking to X, Y, and Z. And now they do. But all those other systems are talking a different language too. So we have a massive technical debt. Every week, with PHP2Shell, the refrigerator attacks, everything. . Every week we turn around and we learn one more way in which there's a huge technical debt that wewe're now in the point where we're like, "oh oops, you know, uh..."

Yes, this is a growing problem. I want to start to wave my arms around and talk about synergistic network effects. I have interviewed some of the people behind the original ARM operating system on The Register and I still attend the meetings of the London Acorn User Group. Over the years they've had some pretty big names in the industry. We had Sophie Wilson, the inventor of the ARM chip, there a couple of times. One time somebody asked a question: "Do you feel happy and proud that there's an ARM chip inside every iPhone and every Android phone?" She laughed at the question, and when the person looked surprised, she said, "There isn't an ARM chip inside every iPhone. There are six or eight ARM chips inside every iPhone." Bear in mind this was more than a decade ago. She said there's a central ARM chip with several cores powering it, but there's an ARM chip in the GSM mobile signaling stack, there's an ARM chip in its USB controller, there's an ARM chip in its memory controller, there's an ARM chip in its Bluetooth controller, because it's cheaper to embed an ARM chip and run a bit of software on it than design dedicated silicon to manage all the different wireless networks. It's all ARM chips all the way down. Your iPhone isn't an ARM device; it's a loose cluster of multiple different ARM devices of different generations. And nobody is entirely sure anymore if they're all running the same stack.

A very visible example of this was in Intel chips until about the early Core 2 Duo era: they had an embedded management processor that was derived from the accelerator in a Nintendo Famicom game from the nineties called Quark. Then Intel replaced it with a cut-down x86 core running Minix, the experimental operating system that inspired Linux. They never gave back any of the code, and the Minix project faltered and is dormant because Dr. Andy Tanenbaum, the guy who founded it, retired. Nowadays in any modern internet-connected server there'll be Linux in its instrumented lights-out monitoring chip. There'll probably be Linux in its network interfaces. There'll be Linux running on the main CPU cluster. I wrote recently about a Linux-powered RISC-V graphics card which runs Ubuntu on loads of RISC-V cores in the GPU.

Are they all on the same Linux version? Have they all been patched against vulnerabilities? No.

Right. So basically the problem goes down to the individual device level.

Yes. There's legions of distributed systems inside your pocket right now, and inside every server. They're running loads of copies of Linux, probably some BSDs, Wind River, ThreadX, QNX, and other embedded operating systems. And some of the same vulnerabilities are in all of them. The Microsoft stack is held together with Linux.

Yes. That's not to say that distributed systems are bad, obviously.

If we had more distributed systems, many of the outages we experienced in the past week wouldn't have been such a problem. But it makes me wonder if there's anything we can do... Can we stop the castle from sinking into the swamp without completely tearing it down and rebuilding it from new foundations? Are we stuck with what we've got?

We can do what they have done in Rome and Istanbul:build a new layer on top.

No, it's not. As vendors, security researchers, and attackers are all using AI to find all these long-hidden vulnerabilities, that creates a massive backlog of software that needs to be patched. Eventually we're going to get to the other side of this where it will make for more secure code and more secure digital infrastructure. Until then, we're going to see more outages. We're going to see more of the same, and it's not going to be very fun for anybody.

Liam, you seem to express some doubt there as to whether it would come out on the other side.

I'm not convinced that this problem is fixable. We have to allow the possibility that maybe they're going to keep finding more holes in this. There's a famous talk by Ken Thompson called "Reflections on Trusting Trust" [PDF]. He embedded a remote access hole intentionally into the original C compiler, and the compiler inserts it into anything it compiles without the code being in the source code of the compiler. You have a compiler which is a binary that runs source code to generate a new binary. The binary can contain the hole, which is never in the source code, as long as it knows to put it in the next one. He did it as an exercise and revealed it at his Turing Award lecture. Stuff as fundamental as that exists because virtually every one of those controller chips has code written in C. And we don't really know what's in all that C, but virtually all of it came from the same early 1970s root of the development of C. There could be nasties lurking in there that are in all of them. They're in all the BSDs, in Linux, and Windows NT is built in C and inherited code from DEC VMS. There could be stuff in there for decades that we have no idea about that's going to crop up, and it's in everything. Some of these devices have no way of being updated; the software's burned in ROMs that are not visible to the operating system that's running. This could keep crumbling away.

I once was a big fan of a website called LoperOS.org by Stanislav Datskovskiy. He was a Lisp evangelist. He's gone very quiet in recent years, but he compared building software out of C to building a model of a bridge or the Eiffel Tower out of toothpicks or matchsticks. The end structure is not very strong because it's mostly weak wood and glue. You build it out of this poor structural material because loads of people can work together on it. And C and tools like C are good at this; you can farm out development to whole teams of people. They're working with tweezers and toothpicks instead of bricks and cement because it's easier to do this over a team.

Somebody said, "If we built houses the way that we build software, then the first termite colony to come along would destroy civilization," because we built it out of bad materials. I'm not personally Christian, but I read the Bible and there's that line about building your house on sand. It doesn't matter how tough you make the house: if you built it on sand and the sand shifts, you've got a big problem.

This problem goes all the way down. This might be a good time to invest in companies developing software in languages like Ada that aren't built on C and don't contain any C whatsoever. When Ada was introduced – Ada is a French language originally from INRIA – it was criticized as being too big and heavy compared to C. But now, compared to C++, it's quite small and quick, and there's a good GNU toolchain and tools like SPARK and AdaCore that have open source development and distribution systems for it. Maybe we're going to have to replace the whole thing.

God, I hope not. One of the things I think about happening is how in past generations of software we slapped new things on top of old things to protect the old things from the new things.

And it makes me wonder if the next version of slapping something on top of our entire infrastructure is AI. We put AI on top of it. We make AI handle bug hunting, vulnerability remediation, and security. It creates a situation where the stuff is safe for now, but software always abstracts layers as you get further up the stack. I wonder if AI is going to be the next level of abstraction to the point where we don't really understand what the code's doing anymore at all.

We just rely on the agents that are running it to handle protecting us. What do you think? Is that a potential next generation that we see here, Jess?

I think it definitely could be. There's a lot of push in the security industry to use AI for both finding and fixing bugs.On the code-writing side of things, it's not there yet. But it's appealing when there's a shortage of human workers who can do this and AI is cheaper. You don't need to pay AI.

Right. Over time. So I think it's likely that is going to be one of the ways we try to solve this problem.

I don't see another way out of it because of the sheer volume of flaws that are being found. Like Liam said, there's low-level stuff getting discovered now that no human would have found, but the fact that an AI found it means someone's going to exploit it at some point.

I think for management this is going to look like a very tempting option, but it will accelerate the problem. We're in an iterative race at the moment – the Red Queen's race. You have to run as  fast as you can to stay where you are. We've got new tools that are finding problems faster than ever, so it's tempting to try and use similar tools to fix them faster than ever, but that means nobody understands the fix. Then if another hole is found deeper down, the whole layer of fixes collapses.

One of the predominant development tools on the PC platform used to be Turbo Pascal. DOS wasn't written in C. Way back when, people accused Microsoft of plagiarizing CP/M. Microsoft didn't write DOS; Tim Paterson of Seattle Computer Products wrote the original. CP/M was written in a high-level language, PL/M, whereas DOS was hand-coded in Assembler. It wasn't plagiarism because they went a level down. In the early days people wrote this stuff in Pascal. I remember Unix catching on and C becoming trendy because it was so fast. For a little while a company called TopSpeed sold a Modula-2 compiler because not only was the code faster than C, but it compiled faster than C compilers back then. Ultimately the sheer inertia of C and C-related languages caught on and all that stuff got sidelined. Borland went through various transitions and Turbo Pascal became Delphi, which went to Embarcadero and is still around, though I'm not sure anybody cares anymore. I worked through one industry shift where Assembler and Pascal-related languages were replaced by C. It could happen again. It wasn't all that bad last time. I know it seems unimaginable now, but I'm not that old. Working in this field for less than four decades, I've watched an entire software industry get swept away and replaced. And we all kept our jobs, and we all kept working on pretty much the same hardware. Maybe that's going to happen again. I know it sounds unimaginable, but it honestly wasn't that bad.

Speaking of hardware, given these outages, connected services going offline are causing chaos. Setting aside the FAA – that's a public service that stranded travelers – banks, Apple, and Microsoft are business problems. We're seeing with AI where everyone is weighing the cost-benefit between hosted services where you pay for tokens versus turning the server closet back into a server closet. Is it time to come back on-premises with a lot of these things? Is it time to run your own Exchange server again or host your own file shares on your own network? It makes me wonder if the solution to some of these outage concerns going forward is going to be a return to on-premises.

Personally I think that's an excellent idea.

I agree, but so many of these companies are entrenched in every other company – Microsoft, for example. It's going to be pretty hard to completely swing to the opposite end of the spectrum here.

Sure. Maybe they need to start offering more self-hosted services again. If you're a business concerned about outages that will probably keep happening,the safest thing to do would be to bring it back on-premises. But if everything you do is in Google or Microsoft 365, it's going to be hard to get yourself out of that, and probably very expensive, at least at first. Especially with the cost of hardware right now not going down given the AI push. So maybe we're all just trapped.

This is part of the digital sovereignty push in Europe at the moment. And it's interesting that on either side of the border between Denmark and northern Germany, there have been two very different stories in the last couple of years. In the last year or so, Schleswig-Holstein has successfully migrated from Microsoft 365 over to Open-Xchange, which is a standards-based email server that can look like and support Outlook. Across the border, Denmark weighed up going all open source. They did a pilot program that failed. They reverted to their Microsoft-based solution just in time to have a massive outage. Have fun.

But you know what, I bet some of this came down to senior government officials saying, "I don't understand this new email client you're showing me. Give me Outlook back, or I'm going to fire the lot of you."" Maybe somebody needs to go in there and say, "We will send somebody around to teach you to use it, or if you're not able to use it, maybe it is time that you give way to somebody who can, because you've just cost us 300 million dollars because you won't change email clients."

We do have standards-based solutions. HTML, SMTP, and IMAP give us standards for moving around email, messages, and documents. We can replace Microsoft-based software iteratively: first the applications, and when people get used to the applications, the operating system. When Ubuntu launched twenty-two years ago, it only filled about half a CD – it took about 300 megabytes – and they wondered what to put on the rest of the CD because in those days they mailed CDs rather than making you download it. So they put Windows installers for all the apps on the CD. You could put it in your Windows box and install LibreOffice, Thunderbird, Firefox, and VLC to get used to the apps. When you were comfortable with the apps, you installed Ubuntu and got the same apps with the new desktop.

You can do this with a government department.

It requires political will, and in America I don't think we have that. So that's a

It's a problem stateside. But the argument that some EU states are making is: why don't we spend hundreds of millions of (insert local currency symbol here) with local companies? We're not claiming we'll save you any money, but we'll keep the money in the country or with an EU partner instead of sending it across the ocean, and we free ourselves of a dependency. That works with senior political types and bureaucrats. This is fixable, but the price may look unacceptable right now to a lot of people. The outages I fear are going to come closer and closer together.

Right. That's going to be the determining factor. It's going to be interesting to watch over the next few months to see what new outages we experience: whether the pace keeps up or increases. We'll see. The US government is overhauling a lot of old systems in aerospace and other sectors, so the push to move to more independent systems or back on-premises is going to be driven by the acceptability of outages.

Yes. "I'm sorry guys, we can't afford to fix it."

Right. What's the pain tolerance? When is it too much, or do people get used to these outages as a part of life? "Today we won't be able to do any work because Microsoft is out again."

Yes. The economic movers and shakers are not going to accept that if it keeps happening. There's going to be a point where the pain tolerance is reached and people say, "No, we can't keep doing this."

You know what? I actually disagree there because, to take a different example: I used to be a motorcyclist. Early in my career I switched from tech support to IT manager to designing and building networks, and I turned up to work on a motorbike. Then I had a really bad crash, switched to three-wheelers, and discovered how bad London traffic had gotten. My injuries prevented me from going back on a solo bike most of the time, but years later I switched to bicycling. You can still cut through traffic very well on a bicycle in a lot of Europe. Car drivers got used to the delays; it gets ten minutes longer to get to work every year, but you don't notice ten minutes over a year, so you put up with it. My next-door neighbor didn't know what underground line he lived on because he drove everywhere. People got used to it taking two or three hours to drive to work and just put up with it. I've seen photos of massive West Coast freeways with eight lanes of stationary traffic. People will put up with amazing levels of delay and non-functionality if it happens gradually enough.

Yes. We will see what comes of everything. You could be right; it could be a slow enough roll that everyone just accepts that we're going to lose some money, but you can't disrupt the tech.

Right. No matter what happens, if there are more outages, we will be here to talk about them on The Kettle. If there are fewer, we probably won't, but one can hope.

Thanks for coming on today, guys, and thank you for listening in. We will talk to you soon.

In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.
